authors: NHS (National Health Service, England)
title: Self-help: generalised anxiety disorder in adults
finding: The NHS self-help advice for anxiety includes regular exercise, relaxation and breathing exercises, good sleep, and cutting down on caffeine and alcohol, which can make anxiety and sleep worse.
strength: moderate: official self-help advice built on research reviews. The advice is general, not tailored to one person.

authors: Singh, B., et al.
title: Effectiveness of physical activity interventions for improving depression, anxiety and distress: an overview of systematic reviews
finding: An overview of 97 reviews (1,039 trials, about 128,000 people) found physical activity reduced symptoms of depression, anxiety and distress compared with usual care, with medium-sized effects.
strength: strong: a very large body of trials. The trials vary a lot in quality and type of exercise.

authors: Noetel, M., et al.
title: Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
finding: Across 218 trials (about 14,000 people), exercise helped depression. Walking or jogging, yoga and strength training did best, especially at higher intensity, and yoga and strength training were well tolerated.
strength: strong: many trials. The authors note most could not blind people to what they were doing, so expectations may add to the effect.

authors: Zaccaro, A., Piarulli, A., Laurino, M., Garbella, E., Menicucci, D., Neri, B., & Gemignani, A.
title: How breath-control can change your life: A systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing
finding: Slow breathing was linked with changes in heart-rate variability and with more comfort, relaxation and alertness and less arousal and anxiety.
strength: moderate: consistent direction, but many included studies were small.

authors: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B.
title: Social relationships and mortality risk: A meta-analytic review
finding: A meta-analysis of 148 studies (308,849 participants) found people with stronger social relationships had about 50% greater odds of survival over the study periods, consistently across age, sex and health status.
strength: strong, large meta-analysis of observational studies. Causation not established

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Anxiety and complementary health approaches: What the science says
finding: NCCIH found some evidence that meditation, music, relaxation techniques and melatonin may ease anxiety, especially around medical procedures, but no complementary approach has been proven to treat anxiety disorders. Acupuncture and massage studies are mixed and often of low quality.
strength: moderate: a careful official summary of reviews. Much of the underlying research is small.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Stress, anxiety, and sleep problems: Considering complementary approaches
finding: A free plain-language guide that goes through relaxation, meditation, music, yoga, melatonin and herbal supplements for stress, anxiety and sleep, with what is known about whether each helps and is safe.
strength: moderate: an official summary for the public. It describes the evidence rather than adding new studies.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Lavender: Usefulness and safety
finding: It is unclear whether lavender aromatherapy helps anxiety, stress, mood or sleep. Short-term use of oral lavender products at the doses studied for anxiety appears reasonably safe. Side effects can include stomach upset, headache and burping.
strength: mixed: oral lavender oil has better evidence than smelling it.

authors: Pittler, M. H., & Ernst, E.
title: Kava extract versus placebo for treating anxiety
venue: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD003383
finding: Across 12 trials, kava extract eased anxiety a little more than a dummy pill, but the effect was small and not robust. The review is now marked as out of date.
strength: mixed: a small effect, and the review is old.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: St. John’s Wort: Usefulness and safety
finding: St John’s wort is not consistently effective for depression and is not approved as a medicine for it in the US. It interacts with many medicines, including birth control pills and some antidepressants, where the mix can cause a dangerous rise in serotonin.
strength: moderate: official summary. Trial results are mixed.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Herb-drug interactions: What the science says
finding: Lists clinically important interactions for St John’s wort, including cyclosporine (a transplant drug), indinavir (an HIV drug), birth control pills, warfarin, digoxin and benzodiazepines.
strength: strong: interactions shown in studies of how the body handles drugs.

authors: Su, K.-P., Tseng, P.-T., Lin, P.-Y., et al.
title: Association of use of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids with changes in severity of anxiety symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 19 trials (2,240 people), omega-3 was linked with less anxiety than control treatments, more clearly in people with a medical or psychiatric condition. The authors said it was too early to call it a first-line treatment.
strength: early: promising, but trials vary.

authors: Marx, W., et al.
title: Effect of saffron supplementation on symptoms of depression and anxiety: A systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 23 trials, saffron eased depression and anxiety symptoms more than a dummy pill. The authors found signs that unhelpful results may be missing, and most trials came from one region.
strength: early: large effects in small trials usually shrink with better studies.

authors: Okereke et al.
title: Effect of long-term vitamin D3 supplementation vs placebo on risk of depression or clinically relevant depressive symptoms and on change in mood scores: A randomized clinical trial
finding: In 18,353 adults aged 50 and over followed for about five years, vitamin D3 (2,000 IU a day) did not lower the risk of depression or improve mood compared with a dummy pill.
strength: strong: a very large, long trial. Most people in it were not low in vitamin D.

authors: Kotera, Y., Richardson, M., & Sheffield, D.
title: Effects of shinrin-yoku (forest bathing) and nature therapy on mental health: A systematic review and meta-analysis
venue: International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction, 20, 337–361
finding: Twenty studies found time in forests and nature therapy eased depression, anxiety and anger in the short term, with the biggest effect on anxiety. The authors asked for more rigorous, longer studies.
strength: early: short-term effects, mixed study quality.

authors: NHS (National Health Service, England)
title: Treatment: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD)
finding: The NHS suggests getting as much natural daylight as you can, exercising and managing stress. Light boxes are not usually provided by public health services. An eye condition, or medicines that make you sensitive to light, can make a light box unsuitable.
strength: early: the NHS says there isn’t enough evidence to be sure light therapy works, though many people find it helps.

authors: Goyal, M., et al.
title: Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: A systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 47 trials (3,515 people), mindfulness programs gave small improvements in anxiety, depression and pain. They were not better than other active treatments such as exercise.
strength: moderate: careful review. Effects were small.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Yoga: Effectiveness and safety
finding: Research suggests yoga may ease anxiety and depression symptoms, but it is unclear whether it helps anxiety disorders. It is generally safe for healthy people with a qualified teacher. Sprains and strains can happen.
strength: early: helpful for symptoms, unclear for disorders.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Tai chi: What you need to know
finding: Tai chi appears safe, with minor aches the most common problem. Research suggests it helps balance in older adults, and NCCIH notes it may improve mood and quality of life in some groups of people with long-term illness.
strength: early: for mood, the research is limited.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Massage therapy: What you need to know
finding: Massage may ease anxiety in some settings, but results are inconsistent and it has not been shown to treat generalized anxiety disorder. Risks are low. Rare serious problems have been reported, mostly with vigorous massage.
strength: mixed: inconsistent results.

authors: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
title: Music and health: What you need to know
finding: Early research suggests music can ease anxiety, for example while waiting for surgery, and in people with cancer, though many studies had a risk of bias.
strength: early: promising, with weaker studies.

authors: NHS (National Health Service, England)
title: Homeopathy
finding: There is no good-quality evidence that homeopathy works for any health condition. NHS England stopped funding it in 2017.
strength: strong: consistent across major reviews.

authors: US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
title: Questions and answers on dietary supplements
finding: In the US, the FDA does not approve dietary supplements before they are sold. Makers are responsible for safety and labels, and the FDA mostly acts after products are on the market.
strength: strong: official description of the law.

authors: NHS (National Health Service, England)
title: Herbal medicines and complementary therapies
finding: NHS advice is to look for the Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) mark and product code on herbal medicines, which show they meet UK standards for safety and quality.
strength: strong: official guidance.

authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), UK
title: Introduction of the Traditional Herbal Registration certification mark
finding: The THR mark shows a herbal medicine is registered with the UK regulator. Registration needs evidence of safety, quality and long traditional use for minor conditions, not clinical trials showing it works.
strength: strong: official description of the scheme.

authors: United States Pharmacopeia (USP)
title: USP’s Dietary Supplement Verification Program
finding: The USP Verified mark means a product was tested to contain what its label says, in the stated amounts, without harmful levels of specified contaminants, and was made under good manufacturing practice. It does not show that the product works.
strength: strong: describes what the testing covers.

authors: NSF
title: Product and ingredient certification (dietary supplements, NSF/ANSI 173)
finding: NSF certification to its dietary supplement standard checks that a product contains what the label says and is screened for specified contaminants, with factory audits and retesting. It is not an approval that the product works.
strength: strong: describes what the testing covers.

authors: Calabrese et al.
title: Effects of a standardized Bacopa monnieri extract on cognitive performance, anxiety, and depression in the elderly
venue: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
finding: Not used on the page.
strength: early
verified_by: Search found the record but not its anxiety results.
note: Bacopa left out of the page: research is mostly about memory. Anxiety evidence is thin and I could not confirm this trial’s anxiety result.

authors: National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia)
title: NHMRC information paper: Evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy for treating health conditions
finding: Not used on the page.
strength: debated
verified_by: Only news and partisan commentary found; the NHMRC page itself was not confirmed.
note: Left out: the NHS homeopathy page covers the same point and was verified.
